This new form of political and factional conflict, with its new participants, would have a major effect on the rise of an intellectual and “ideological” movement. As we shall see, that movement became one of the main forces pushing Arab thought into new areas of rational inquiry, where the first seeds of Arab-Islamic philosophical thought would begin to grow.

Now that we have finished the first part of this study, we should pause for a general review of its main themes. This will help us preserve the unity and sequence of the argument and keep sight of our main purpose.

Our aim is to follow the historical process through which Arab thought developed alongside Arab society itself: from the pre-Islamic period, through the rise of Islam, and eventually into the Abbasid age, when Arab philosophy flourished alongside the experimental sciences, the rational sciences, and major changes in social relations.
We use the phrase “historical process” because we believe that Arab philosophy, when it finally emerged, was the mature result of much earlier intellectual seeds.

Those seeds were connected to roots already growing in Arab and Islamic societies. They developed within a historical setting shaped by social, political, religious, and cultural forces, all of which came together within the continuous process we have been describing.
For that reason, we have tried to study the concrete features of this philosophy in a way that follows the logic of the historical reality from which we believe it emerged.
This does not mean, of course, that we ignore the outside influences that later flowed into this process and helped turn it into a great river that continued for centuries.

What we mean is that we want to follow this river from its earliest springs, however small and limited they may first have been, until other streams began flowing into it from many directions, carrying the cultures of different peoples and rich elements from many civilizations.

In fact, when we say that Arab-Islamic philosophy belongs to the environments of Arab life itself, this already includes recognition of those outside influences. Arab life had by then become deeply mixed with the lives of the other peoples with whom the Arabs had come into contact through the same historical process.
We have deliberately paused to make this point because we want to preserve the connection between all parts of this study, from beginning to end.
Following the logic of the historical reality we have adopted, we therefore had to begin with the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam.

This allowed us to look for Arab thought at its earliest visible sources, or in its earliest seeds. In other words, we began where the visible part of the long historical process that eventually led to philosophy first comes into view.

We have left aside the still earlier and much less visible part of that history, which stretches back for centuries before the Common Era, to the period when the ancient Arab states that later disappeared were still in existence.
This is the point from which our general review of Part One now begins.
What mattered to us in studying the pre-Islamic period was to see how Arab life was changing at that stage, the direction in which it was moving, and the role played by thought in that movement.
As far as we were able to determine, Chapter One led us to the following conclusions.

First: The people of the Arabian Peninsula had long maintained trading relationships with peoples at either end of the commercial routes that carried goods through Arabia along two major international routes.
Over time, these relationships went beyond the exchange of material goods and became channels of cultural interaction as well.
The Arabs did not remain mere carriers of other people’s goods. By the period immediately before Islam, they had become owners both of merchandise and of the means used to transport it.

This led to the rise of merchant groups and to the growth of many towns. Older settlements that had once been little more than large villages also expanded. Mecca, after developing into an important commercial center, came to be called the “Mother of Cities.”
This development also made it possible for some Arabs to become owners of agricultural land.
Byzantine gold coins and Persian silver coins came into widespread circulation across different parts of the peninsula.

At the same time, distinct social groups emerged whose wealth set them apart from the rest of society. They could accumulate money, merchandise, and valuable property, and they could exploit those who lacked such resources.

They employed poorer people in commercial caravans, agriculture, domestic service, and small crafts. They also lent money at extremely high rates of interest, or usury, placing borrowers under severe pressure.
This new social differentiation began to weaken the older system that had dominated the peninsula: the primitive tribal order.

A clearer division of labor appeared, along with early signs of class division. The exact form differed between the desert and the towns, especially Mecca, which had become the most developed center of this new class structure.
Second: This new social order inevitably began to create a political form suited to it.
That form appeared most clearly in Mecca, where social tensions had become sharper than elsewhere.
The leaders of Quraysh gathered in the Dār al-Nadwa, the assembly house where they discussed the organization of civic, economic, and religious affairs.
We regarded this as an early, embryonic form of the state.
The Dār al-Nadwa combined legislative and executive powers. Those powers belonged exclusively to the wealthy leaders, who imposed their decisions on the weaker and poorer sections of society.
Third: Religious life in this pre-Islamic society reflected both its intellectual condition and its social structure.
Religious ideas expressed new ways of thinking about relations between human beings, on the one hand, and between humanity, the universe, and nature, on the other.
We saw the social side of these religious developments appear in two main forms.
The first was the way the wealthy leaders of Mecca concentrated religious authority in their own hands and in their own city.
The Kaaba stood there, containing the idols of many tribes, whose members came on pilgrimage at particular times each year. These religious seasons also became commercial markets.

Religious leadership therefore gave the wealthy of Mecca a material basis for protecting their economic interests. It became an important source of profit and wealth and strengthened their “class” power.
The second form appeared in various local movements calling for people to abandon idol worship and worship instead a single, universal, invisible God.
The wealthy of Mecca opposed these movements because, at least in the short term, they threatened both their leadership and their material interests.
The conflict between Judaism and Christianity was another example of the way social struggles could appear in religious form.

We are referring especially to the conflict that developed in Yemen toward the end of the sixth century. It was clearly less a religious struggle than a conflict between local rulers and the Abyssinians, who wanted to control Yemen in the name of Christianity and were backed by the Byzantine state.
Religious life also had an intellectual side that appeared, on the surface at least, to have a degree of independence from these social conditions.

The various religious movements, along with spiritual and religious reflections, appeared in the sayings of the “wise men,” a recognized group in pre-Islamic Arabia; in the speeches of soothsayers; in the ideas of some poets; in widely repeated proverbs; and in certain myths.
All of these expressed new intellectual tendencies. They were accompanied by a simple form of rational debate, still at a very early level.

We can see examples of this kind of debate in the Qurʾan, when it describes the objections raised by Muhammad’s pre-Islamic opponents against the beliefs he preached during the earliest phase of the Islamic mission.
These objections show that some people in pre-Islamic Arabia had already developed forms of reflective thought about the nature of existence.
Some of them even seem to have thought about existence in a way resembling the natural philosophers of ancient Greece.
Muslims later called such people Dahriyya, because the Qurʾan describes them as saying:
“There is nothing but our first life. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time.”

In their different forms, these religious developments were the clearest cultural and intellectual expressions of the changes taking place in pre-Islamic Arab life as society moved toward a new stage of social and intellectual development.
At the same time, another area had developed to a striking degree: artistic expression, especially poetic language.
Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry remained a model even during later Islamic periods that were far more socially and intellectually developed.

This allowed us to conclude that this form of artistic expression, together with the remarkable richness of its language, must have been connected to a much longer earlier history. That history was not completely broken by the historical rupture between the ancient civilization of Arabia and the pre-Islamic period we are discussing here.
We devoted Chapter Two of Part One to the period in which Islam arose.
Our examination of the beliefs introduced by Islam, the laws it established, and the many questions raised by this major event in Arab society led us to the following conclusions.
First: The new religion, Islam, had a clearly historical character.
This was true not only of its social message and religious beliefs, but also of many of its religious forms and doctrines.
In other words, Islam developed out of social, religious, and intellectual tendencies already moving within pre-Islamic society and pushing it toward historical change.
Islam expressed forms of human consciousness that could develop at that particular stage of human history—and not only of Arab history.
We also saw this historical character in the artistic form of Islam’s great central text, the Qurʾan.

The Qurʾanic text appeared as a remarkable and powerful development of the Arabic art of expression, which, as we have already seen, had reached a high level during the pre-Islamic period immediately before the rise of Islam.
Muslims regarded the Qurʾan as divine revelation and believed that human beings were incapable of producing anything like it.
Yet even with this belief, Muslims did not deny that the Qurʾan used the forms of Arabic eloquence itself, though in a form they regarded as higher, purer, and more magnificent.
There is no doubt that this is true.
But it also supports our argument that the Qurʾanic text has a historical character, in the sense that it represents the continued development of a cultural form already present in pre-Islamic life.
Second: Many of the beliefs preached by Islam were also found in Judaism, Christianity, and the Ḥanīf tradition.

These included beliefs about the creation of the universe, the Creator, one God, the coming into existence of the world, the afterlife, and resurrection, together with a strong rejection of idol worship.
In presenting its religious beliefs, the Qurʾan also addressed many questions that were already being widely debated in pre-Islamic society.
All of this supports the conclusion we reached in Chapter Two: Islam emerged from its own society and its own historical period.
It did not arrive on earth cut off from its historical relationship with this world—or, at the very least, with the part of the world in which it first appeared.
Third: These same religious beliefs contained, beneath their religious form, an expression of the level that social consciousness had reached among the people of that society.
We explained this through the principles of monotheism and resurrection.
We saw monotheism as a metaphysical expression of a real social development.

The new class divisions emerging in pre-Islamic society were beginning to break apart the narrow framework of tribal organization and create the need for a broader social framework capable of bringing people together into larger and more unified communities.
We interpreted the principle of resurrection in a similar way.

It gave metaphysical expression to the hopes of the poor masses: on the one hand, for compensation for the hardship of their material lives, and on the other, for justice against the higher social groups whose wealth set them apart or who oppressed them through exploitation.
Fourth: Many of the social laws introduced by Islam directly reflected the objective social conditions of the time.
They attempted to reduce the material suffering of the poor by banning usury and monopoly and by imposing certain taxes on the wealthy.
Islam also introduced laws regulating social relations, including relations connected with production.
But these laws remained within the basic framework of private property and the class differences that arose from it.

Fifth: Islam established a “theory” of knowledge, including knowledge of the general principles and rules of religious law, in which divine revelation was treated as the only source of those principles.
Human beings, meanwhile, were limited to knowledge gained through the senses and to the direct, purely empirical knowledge that sensory experience could provide.
In this way, Islam created a reciprocal relationship between knowledge and faith.
Within this framework, rational knowledge available to human beings could go no further than using sensory knowledge to support religious belief.
It was therefore natural for us to conclude that Islam closed the way to intellectual debate over matters of faith and questions concerning the world beyond nature.
Islamic texts do not leave this conclusion unsupported.
The Qurʾan and sayings attributed to the Prophet contain passages that either forbid or discourage debate over such questions.

But when Arab thought found this route to further development blocked, it turned in another direction: toward independent legal reasoning based on personal judgment in applying the general rules and principles of Islamic law.

It followed this path until historical conditions made it possible to reopen the first path as well—the path of rational debate over questions of faith and over the metaphysical nature of the universe.
After the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, political and sectarian struggles became more intense. From those struggles came the living seeds of philosophical thought.
Those seeds then developed naturally within Arab-Islamic life until, in the ninth century CE, they produced what became known as Arab philosophy.
C — The Age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We devoted Chapter Three of Part One to the most important historical developments of this period.
These developments created the setting in which different forms of religious conflict and later political and sectarian conflict took shape.
This conflict matters to our study because, once the Umayyad period began, much of it developed into an intellectual and “ideological” struggle.

Other intellectual and ideological currents either became part of this struggle or developed alongside it. These included the Muʿtazila, the current represented by the ideas of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, the Qadariyya, and others.
